comparator.name: Physics
comparator.sourceNotes: The current full-time standalone Physics ledger has 60 EC in year one, 51 required plus 9 restricted in year two, and 30 open profile, 3 restricted and 27 research-related EC in year three. The example uses Experimental Projects and Fluid Phenomena in Soft Matter in year two and Relativistic Electrodynamics in year three. Experimental Projects requires a team and advance project discussion. Fluid Phenomena recommends analysis and statistical physics. Relativistic Electrodynamics assumes both introductory analysis courses, both linear algebra courses and Classical Electrodynamics. Research normally follows completion of years one and two and requires study-adviser approval. The adviser assesses exceptions for outstanding courses. The standard project runs 17 weeks in a Leiden physics group, primarily in experimental physics. The 27 EC block comprises the 20 EC project, 3 EC thesis, 1 EC presentation and 3 EC research skills and integrity.

alternativeSelection.assessment: One qualified response is supported. Mathematical and experimental work on waves, materials, natural systems and energy addresses the use of mathematics to explain physical phenomena and the behaviour of matter and energy. The strongest coherent pathway combines theory, modelling and instrument-based work, followed by resource and renewable-system projects. The physics content has enough recurring weight to support a qualified comparison. It remains narrower in mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum and statistical physics, and lacks a continuous sequence of physics labs and independent physics research. A fundamental-physics route lacks the advanced subject sequence. A distinct experimental route would depend on the same wave, materials and geophysical work and lacks advanced physics instrumentation and supervised laboratory research. A computational route centred on AI would shift from physical phenomena toward generic algorithms and reuse the strongest mathematical courses.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both use mathematics to describe motion. UCR models the movement of robot joints and arms, while Leiden develops Newtonian mechanics, forces and conservation laws.
Both use Python to solve problems. Leiden integrates it with numerical physics and experimental data throughout the degree.
Both develop single-variable differentiation and integration for scientific models. UCR also uses numerical approximation and differential equations in a modelling project.
Both use systems of equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both develop calculus for functions of several variables.
Both use differential equations and Fourier methods. UCR applies them to signals and systems. Leiden also studies partial differential equations and complex analysis.
UCR applies electrical resistivity and electromagnetic methods to soils and aquifers. Leiden develops the underlying theory of electric and magnetic fields.
Both study interference and other wave behaviour. UCR uses oscilloscopes and optical spectra, while Leiden develops optics in greater depth, including lenses and diffraction.
Leiden begins its experimental-physics laboratory sequence here.
Leiden continues experimental physics in a second first-year laboratory course.
Leiden introduces modern physics in a dedicated course.

Leiden teaches presentation and communication in a dedicated physics component. UCR develops these skills across courses.
Leiden continues analytical mechanics in a second course.
Leiden develops physics measurement and experiment design through a dedicated lab sequence.
Leiden uses statistical mechanics to explain thermodynamic behaviour. UCR studies probability and statistics separately.
Leiden continues linear algebra with more abstract methods and applications in physics.
Leiden studies the physics of solids. UCR studies selected material properties in sustainability applications.

The Leiden elective asks a team to design and carry out an experimental physics project.
Leiden’s elective studies viscosity and capillarity in soft materials. UCR studies water and sediments in Earth science.

notes.text: Leiden develops a sustained sequence in mechanics, optics, electromagnetism, quantum and statistical physics, and laboratory research. UCR applies selected physical principles to materials, Earth processes and renewable energy. Leiden requires a physics research project. Independent research at UCR is optional and sits outside the displayed schedule.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Physics degree studies matter, motion, energy and fields through mathematical theory, experiments and computation. Students finish with a project in a physics research group.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR option develops mathematical and computational tools and uses them to study waves, materials, Earth systems and renewable energy. It includes applied laboratory and field measurements.

curriculum.limitation: The example includes 9 EC of restricted electives in year two, and 30 EC of elective study and a 3 EC restricted elective in year three. The 27 EC research block normally follows completion of the first two years and requires study-adviser approval.
